mcqs.question: What is the fundamental trade-off along the CPU → GPU → ASIC specialization spectrum?
options: Generality is traded for efficiency at a narrower set of tasks as you move toward the ASIC end
Cost decreases while clock speed increases
Power consumption always increases as you specialize further
mcqs.explanation: The core trade-off is generality for efficiency at a narrower task set. Cost and clock speed aren't the defining axis, power for the target task typically decreases (not increases) with specialization, and programmability decreases (not increases) toward the ASIC end.

mcqs.question: What makes a systolic array well-suited to matrix multiplication specifically?
options: It uses higher clock speeds than a GPU to brute-force the computation
Matrix multiply has a highly regular, predictable dataflow that can be hardwired into a fixed grid of multiply-accumulate cells passing data to neighbors, eliminating most instruction-level overhead
It stores the entire matrix in on-chip cache, avoiding memory access entirely
It uses the same warp-based scheduling as a GPU, just with more warps
mcqs.explanation: Systolic arrays exploit matrix multiply's fixed, regular dataflow pattern by hardwiring it into silicon rather than fetching/decoding instructions per step. Clock speed isn't the mechanism, cache alone doesn't explain the efficiency gain, and systolic arrays don't use warp-based scheduling — that's a GPU-specific concept.

mcqs.question: A team is rapidly iterating on novel, unconventional model architectures for research. Why might they prefer a GPU over a TPU/ML ASIC despite the ASIC's better efficiency?
options: GPUs are always cheaper to purchase than TPUs
TPUs cannot perform any floating-point computation
The GPU's general programmability lets them run arbitrary new kernels and custom ops that a narrowly-tuned ASIC may not support well
GPUs have larger global memory capacity in all cases
mcqs.explanation: The core reason is flexibility: GPUs can run novel kernels that don't fit an ASIC's narrow target operations. Cost and memory capacity vary by specific hardware generation rather than being a fixed rule, and TPUs do support floating-point computation.

mcqs.question: Why is it inaccurate to describe an ML ASIC like a TPU as simply 'a faster GPU'?
options: Because TPUs actually run slower than GPUs on every workload
Because 'faster' is not a meaningful term in computer architecture
Because ASICs cannot be manufactured using the same process nodes as GPUs
Because an ASIC typically supports a much narrower set of operations than a GPU's general programmability, so it can perform poorly or not run at all outside its targeted operations
mcqs.explanation: The narrowness of an ASIC's supported operations, not raw speed, is what distinguishes it from a GPU — the same specialization that buys efficiency also caps generality. ASICs are typically faster at their target op (not slower), can use comparable process nodes, and 'faster' is a perfectly meaningful (if incomplete) description here.
